sections.heading: Three-headed Geryon and Echidna
sections.translation:
Chrysaor fathered three-headed Geryon
with Callirhoe, daughter of Oceanus,
the famous river god who circles the world.
Mighty Heracles killed Geryon
beside his cattle with their rolling walk,
on Erytheia, an island surrounded by water.
That day he drove the broad-browed cattle
to the sacred city of Tiryns,
crossing the stream of Oceanus,
after killing Orthus, the watchdog,
and Eurytion, the cattle herder,
in their misty cattle shelter beyond famous Oceanus.

She also bore another monster, impossible to overcome,
nothing like mortal humans or the deathless gods:
fierce-hearted, divine Echidna, born in a hollow cave.
Half of her was a nymph, a female nature spirit,
with lovely cheeks and lively eyes;
the other half was a monstrous snake, huge and dreadful,
with a dappled skin, eating flesh raw
in the hidden depths of the sacred earth.
Her cave lies beneath a hollow rock,
far from deathless gods and mortal humans.
There the gods assigned her a splendid home.
There dreadful Echidna keeps watch underground,
in the land of the Arimoi—
a nymph who never dies or grows old, through all her days.
sections.summary: Heracles kills three-headed Geryon and takes his cattle. Echidna, half beautiful nymph and half terrifying snake, lives forever in a cave underground.

cards.label: Chrysaor
cards.general: A mythical figure whose name means “Golden Sword.”
cards.here: He fathers Geryon with Callirhoe.

cards.label: Geryon
cards.general: A three-headed being who owns a herd of cattle.
cards.here: Heracles kills him and drives away his cattle.

cards.label: Callirhoe
cards.general: A daughter of the river god Oceanus.
cards.here: She is Geryon’s mother.

cards.label: Oceanus
cards.general: The divine river imagined as flowing around the world.
cards.here: Heracles crosses his stream to bring the cattle home.

cards.label: Heracles
cards.general: A Greek hero famous for his enormous strength; also called Hercules.
cards.here: He kills Geryon, Orthus, and Eurytion and takes the cattle.

cards.label: Erytheia
cards.general: A mythical island beyond Oceanus.
cards.here: Geryon and his cattle are there.

cards.label: Tiryns
cards.general: An ancient Greek city associated with Heracles.
cards.here: Heracles brings the cattle to this sacred city.

cards.label: Orthus
cards.general: Geryon’s monstrous watchdog.
cards.here: Heracles kills him at the cattle shelter.

cards.label: Eurytion
cards.general: The herder who looks after Geryon’s cattle.
cards.here: Heracles kills him alongside Orthus.

cards.label: Echidna
cards.general: An immortal creature, half woman and half snake.
cards.here: She lives underground, far from gods and humans.

cards.label: Nymph
cards.general: A female divine spirit connected with nature.
cards.here: Echidna’s upper half looks like a beautiful nymph.

cards.label: Arimoi
cards.general: A people or region whose location is uncertain.
cards.here: Echidna’s underground home is in their land.

sections.heading: A Family of Monsters
sections.translation:
They say Typhaon, a monstrous being,
terrible, violent, and lawless,
joined in love with that bright-eyed girl, Echidna.
She became pregnant and bore fierce-hearted children.

First she bore Orthus, the dog who served Geryon.
Then came Cerberus, a monster beyond description,
impossible to overcome: the raw-flesh-eating dog
of Hades, god of the dead,
with a voice like bronze and fifty heads,
merciless and strong.
Third she bore the Hydra of Lerna,
a water monster skilled in deadly harm.
The white-armed goddess Hera raised her,
in boundless anger at mighty Heracles.
But Heracles, son of Zeus, the chief god,
and known as Amphitryon’s son,
killed her with pitiless bronze,
helped by Iolaus, who loved battle,
and guided by Athena, goddess of battle and its spoils.

She also bore the Chimera, breathing unstoppable fire,
terrible and huge, swift-footed and strong.
She had three heads: one a fierce-eyed lion’s,
one a goat’s, and one a snake’s—a mighty serpent’s.
Pegasus, the winged horse, and brave Bellerophon
brought her down.

After mating with Orthus, she bore the deadly Sphinx,
a monster that brought ruin to the people of Thebes,
and the lion of Nemea.
Hera, Zeus’s glorious wife, raised that lion
and settled him in Nemea’s hills, a curse on humans.
Living there, he ravaged the local people,
ruling over Tretus, Nemea, and Apesas.
But mighty Heracles used his strength to bring him down.

Ceto, a sea goddess, joined in love with Phorcys,
a sea god, and bore her youngest child:
a dreadful snake that guards the all-golden apples
in the dark earth’s hidden places, at its vast outer limits.
Such are the offspring of Ceto and Phorcys.
sections.summary: Echidna’s family includes terrifying dogs, the Hydra, and other monsters. Heroes defeat several of them. Ceto and Phorcys also have a snake that guards golden apples.

cards.label: Typhaon
cards.general: A powerful monstrous being, also called Typhon.
cards.here: He mates with Echidna and fathers her first children.

cards.label: Orthus
cards.general: The monstrous dog that guards Geryon’s cattle.
cards.here: He is Echidna’s first child and later fathers two monsters.

cards.label: Cerberus
cards.general: The dog of the underworld, where the dead go.
cards.here: Hesiod gives him fifty heads and a voice like bronze.

cards.label: Hades
cards.general: The god who rules the dead; his name can also mean his realm.
cards.here: Cerberus is his dog.

cards.label: Hydra of Lerna
cards.general: A dangerous water monster associated with Lerna in Greece.
cards.here: Hera raises her, and Heracles kills her with help.

cards.label: Hera
cards.general: A major goddess and the wife of Zeus.
cards.here: She raises the Hydra out of hatred for Heracles and also raises the Nemean lion.

cards.label: Heracles
cards.general: A famously strong hero, born to Zeus and a human mother.
cards.here: He defeats the Hydra and the Nemean lion.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The chief Greek god.
cards.here: He is Heracles’s father and Hera’s husband.

cards.label: Amphitryon
cards.general: The human husband of Heracles’s mother.
cards.here: Heracles is called his son as well as Zeus’s son.

cards.label: Iolaus
cards.general: A companion of Heracles.
cards.here: He helps Heracles kill the Hydra.

cards.label: Athena
cards.general: A goddess of wisdom, skilled action, and warfare.
cards.here: Her guidance helps Heracles defeat the Hydra.

cards.label: Bronze
cards.general: A metal used for ancient weapons, armor, and other objects.
cards.here: It describes Cerberus’s ringing voice and stands for Heracles’s weapon.

cards.label: Chimera
cards.general: A fire-breathing monster combining different animals.
cards.here: She has the heads of a lion, a goat, and a snake.

cards.label: Pegasus and Bellerophon
cards.general: Pegasus is a winged horse; Bellerophon is a human hero.
cards.here: Together they defeat the Chimera.

cards.label: Sphinx
cards.general: A female monster associated with the Greek city of Thebes.
cards.here: She brings destruction to its people, called Cadmeans in the Greek.

cards.label: Nemean lion
cards.general: A monstrous lion associated with Nemea in Greece.
cards.here: He terrorizes the surrounding area until Heracles defeats him.

cards.label: Tretus, Nemea, and Apesas
cards.general: Neighboring places in Greece: a mountain pass, a valley, and a mountain.
cards.here: They mark the territory dominated by the lion.

cards.label: Ceto and Phorcys
cards.general: Ancient sea divinities who are parents of several monsters.
cards.here: Their youngest child is the snake guarding the golden apples.

cards.label: Golden apples
cards.general: Precious mythical fruit kept at the far edge of the world.
cards.here: A dreadful snake guards them; this passage gives the snake no name.

uncertainties: The mother meant by “she” in line 295 is disputed. Ceto and Callirhoe are possible referents; the translation leaves her unnamed.
The “she” who bears the Chimera in line 319 may be Echidna or the Hydra. The “she” who mates with Orthus in lines 326–327 may be Echidna or the Chimera. The translation preserves these uncertainties.

Lines 323–324 are marked for deletion in the supplied Greek and are omitted from the translation. They describe the Chimera as lion in front, serpent behind, and goat in the middle, breathing blazing fire.
The location of the Arimoi is uncertain.
